params.question: A 3-year-old child recovering from bacterial meningitis fails a hearing screening test. Which of the following best explains the mechanism of this complication?

answers.text: Ototoxicity from aminoglycoside antibiotics used during treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although aminoglycosides can be ototoxic, the hearing loss here is a direct sequela of meningitis — inflammatory exudate in the subarachnoid space damages the vestibulocochlear nerve.

answers.text: Direct bacterial invasion and destruction of the organ of Corti

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The primary mechanism is not direct bacterial invasion of the cochlea. Rather, the purulent exudate filling the subarachnoid space causes inflammatory damage to cranial nerve VIII as it passes through.

answers.text: Inflammatory damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve as it traverses the inflamed subarachnoid space

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cranial nerve VIII passes through the subarachnoid space, where purulent exudate accumulates in bacterial meningitis. This inflammatory environment damages the nerve, causing sensorineural hearing loss.

answers.text: Obstruction of the cochlear aqueduct by fibrinous exudate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fibrinous exudate does obstruct CSF pathways — but at the arachnoid villi, causing communicating hydrocephalus. Hearing loss results from direct inflammatory damage to the vestibulocochlear nerve.

overallFeedback.feedback: Sensorineural hearing loss in bacterial meningitis results from inflammatory damage to cranial nerve VIII (vestibulocochlear) as it traverses the subarachnoid space filled with purulent exudate — it is the commonest long-term sequela in children.

The vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is the cranial nerve most often damaged in bacterial meningitis because it runs through the subarachnoid space where purulent exudate collects. Sensorineural hearing loss is the commonest long-term sequela in children.

params.question: In tubercular meningitis, the characteristic basal exudate develops following the rupture of which structure?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms are found in small penetrating arteries and are associated with hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage, not tubercular meningitis.
The Ghon complex is the primary pulmonary tuberculosis lesion (Ghon focus plus draining lymph node). The CNS equivalent is the Rich focus — a small tuberculoma in the brain or meninges.

A Rich focus is a small tuberculoma in the brain parenchyma or meninges. Its rupture releases tuberculoprotein into the subarachnoid space, producing the dense basal exudate that is the hallmark of TB meningitis.
Arachnoid granulations are sites of CSF reabsorption into dural venous sinuses. Their blockage by exudate causes hydrocephalus, but they are not the source of the tubercular exudate.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the pathogenesis of TB meningitis: it begins with rupture of a Rich focus (a small tuberculoma in the brain or meninges), releasing tuberculoprotein into the subarachnoid space and producing the characteristic dense exudate at the base of the brain.

The Rich focus — a small caseous tuberculoma in the brain or meninges — is the starting point of TB meningitis. Its rupture floods the subarachnoid space with tuberculoprotein, producing the characteristic basal exudate, granulomatous inflammation, and sequelae including hydrocephalus and cranial nerve palsies.

params.question: A biopsy from a posterior fossa tumour in a 6-year-old child shows small round blue cells arranged around a central fibrillary core with no true lumen. Which tumour does this histological pattern characterise?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Retinoblastoma shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes with a true central lumen and is an intraocular tumour, not a posterior fossa mass.

Oligodendroglioma shows the 'fried-egg' appearance — round nuclei with clear perinuclear halos in a chicken-wire vascular pattern. It typically arises in the frontal lobe of adults, not the posterior fossa of children.
Meningioma shows concentric whorls of meningothelial cells and psammoma bodies (laminated calcified rings). It is a benign extra-axial tumour seen predominantly in adults.

Homer-Wright rosettes — small round blue cells around a fibrillary neuropil core with no true lumen — are diagnostic of medulloblastoma, the most common malignant brain tumour in children, arising in the cerebellar vermis.

overallFeedback.feedback: A posterior fossa tumour in a child showing small round blue cells in rosettes without a true lumen points to medulloblastoma — distinguish Homer-Wright rosettes (no lumen, fibrillary core) from Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes (true lumen, seen in retinoblastoma).

Homer-Wright rosettes with a fibrillary core and no true lumen are the hallmark of medulloblastoma. It arises in the cerebellar vermis of children, and among its molecular subtypes, WNT-activated carries the best prognosis.

params.question: According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, why does hereditary retinoblastoma typically present bilaterally while sporadic cases are almost always unilateral?

answers.text: Hereditary tumours are more aggressive and spread to the contralateral eye via the optic chiasm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bilaterality in hereditary retinoblastoma is not due to tumour spread between eyes. It occurs because every retinal cell already carries one mutant RB1 allele, raising the probability of a second hit occurring in either eye.

answers.text: In hereditary cases, one RB1 allele is already mutated in every cell from birth, so only one additional somatic hit in any retinal cell completes the requirement

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The germline mutation provides the first hit in every cell. Only one further somatic event in any retinal cell — in either eye — is needed to inactivate both RB1 alleles, making bilateral, multifocal, and earlier-onset disease likely.

answers.text: Sporadic retinoblastoma arises from a different tumour-suppressor gene that affects only one eye

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both hereditary and sporadic retinoblastoma involve the same RB1 gene on chromosome 13q14. The difference is whether the first hit is inherited (germline) or acquired (somatic), not a different gene.

answers.text: Bilateral presentation requires homozygous germline deletion of both RB1 alleles from conception

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Complete loss of both RB1 alleles in the germline would be embryonically lethal. Hereditary cases carry a heterozygous germline mutation in one allele; the second allele is lost somatically in the tumour cell.

overallFeedback.feedback: In hereditary retinoblastoma, a germline mutation provides the first hit in every cell. Only one additional somatic mutation in any retinal cell completes the two-hit requirement, making bilateral disease likely. In sporadic cases, two independent somatic hits must occur in the same cell — a much rarer event, hence unilateral disease.

Knudson's two-hit hypothesis explains that hereditary retinoblastoma is bilateral because every cell already carries one mutant RB1 allele from birth — only one additional somatic event in any retinal cell is needed. This principle applies to all tumour-suppressor genes.
